draft.title: Drawing a cross-section
card: A cross-section shows the shape of the land along a line drawn on a map. It is like a side view of the land, as if it were sliced open.
First, draw a line on the map between two points. Then mark each place where a contour line crosses it, and write that contour's height.
Next, draw a graph with distance along the bottom and height up the side. Plot a point for each mark, at its distance and its height.
Join the points with a smooth line. The line rises where the land climbs and falls where the land drops.
draft.remember: Mark each contour crossing, plot its height, then join the points.

a.q: Which two pieces of information are plotted for each point on a cross-section?
opts: Distance along the line and height of the contour
Compass direction and width of the contour
Distance along the line and the type of land use
Height of the contour and the map's scale bar
a.why: Each point sits at its distance along the line and at the height of the contour that crosses there. Land use is not plotted on a cross-section.
a.clue: The graph has distance along the bottom and one other measure up the side.

b.q: Tom draws a line across a map of a ridge near Hobart. The contours it crosses are 100 m, 200 m, 300 m, 200 m, then 100 m. What shape does his cross-section have?
opts: A hill that rises to a peak and then falls
A valley that falls to a low point and then rises
A flat plain at a steady height of 200 m
A slope that rises steadily from start to finish
b.why: The heights go up to 300 m and then come back down, so the line rises to a peak and falls. A valley would need the heights to fall first and then rise.
b.clue: Follow the heights in order and see whether they go up, down or both.

a.best: Distance along the line and height of the contour

b.best: A hill that rises to a peak and then falls

problems.detail: The stem says the map shows 'a ridge', which tells the student the land is raised and gives away the hill answer without reading the heights. A neutral phrase such as 'a map of land near Hobart' would avoid this.

check.summary: The card and both answers are correct. Question b's stem calls the land 'a ridge', which hints at the hill answer, so that word should be removed.
